strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: inexpensive valuation of candidate fine-tuning data for large language and vision-language models. Computing scores from hidden states and prediction errors avoids backpropagation and repeated training.
The scoring rule is explicit, and its matrix formulation and batching algorithm make the core method understandable and implementable.

Experiments cover multiple model families, text and multimodal tasks, and scaling up to 72B parameters. Results demonstrate strong same-class retrieval, while the embedding-only ablation supports the usefulness of prediction-error information.
The reported runtime reductions are practically promising. Dataset sizes, templates, hardware, and some baseline training settings are documented.
weaknesses: The central influence claim is not directly validated. Evaluation treats membership in the same class as ground-truth influence, without measuring actual validation-loss changes after updates, removal, or reweighting, or downstream gains from data selection. Shared templates, task-specific chatbot names, and explicit style labels in captions make these benchmarks particularly susceptible to lexical and task-identity matching. Strong retrieval performance therefore does not establish accurate training influence.

The theoretical guarantee applies to a restrictive surrogate parameterization. Equation (2) is exactly the inner product of log-likelihood gradients with respect to the output matrix W, computed analytically. The proof treats each distinct context's hidden representation as an independently trainable parameter, eliminating cross-example representation updates. Actual transformers share parameters across contexts, including under the evaluated attention-layer LoRA setup. Distinct inputs do not eliminate those interactions. No approximation bound or empirical validation bridges this gap. Appendix 8.2 also reverses the interpretation of the two terms: Term (I) comes from gradients with respect to W, contrary to the accompanying explanation.

The mislabeled-data evaluation does not directly measure binary corruption detection. Appendix 8.3 defines positives as clean examples sharing the validation example's class, while negatives include both corrupted examples and clean examples from other classes. This measures a mixture of relevance and cleanliness. Direct corruption-detection metrics and a simple pretrained-model loss or label-confidence baseline are needed to support the stated detection claim.

The vocabulary restriction introduces an untested approximation. Probability mass need not concentrate on words appearing in the observed batch, and changing batch composition changes which coordinates contribute to a pair's score. There is no full-vocabulary comparison, approximation-error analysis, or batch-size and batch-composition sensitivity study.

Important evaluation and reproduction details remain unspecified: the cutoff and denominator for 'Recall,' the meaning of reported uncertainties, random seeds, scoring batch sizes, and several baseline implementation settings. The stated Recall definition resembles precision at a cutoff unless an additional convention is imposed. Some textual claims also contradict Table 2: For-Value does not achieve the highest subject-generation recall on Qwen, and its Llama improvement over HyperINF is 6.6 percentage points rather than over 7.

The efficiency evidence needs more precise accounting. Table 3 omits sequence length, validation-set size, and forward feature-extraction costs, so it does not characterize end-to-end complexity. Runtime comparisons use different GPU configurations and extrapolate some baseline measurements; separating inference, scoring, and training costs would make the speedup claim more interpretable. Overall, the unresolved influence-validity and reproducibility issues prevent a sound Findings recommendation despite the promising retrieval results.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical problem: estimating data value for large pretrained LLMs and VLMs without expensive retraining or backpropagation. The proposed score is explicit, straightforward to implement, and applicable to both modalities.

Equation (2) provides a useful computational formulation of output-layer gradient similarity using hidden states and prediction residuals obtained from forward passes. The comparison with the embedding-only ablation supports the usefulness of incorporating prediction errors on the evaluated tasks.

The reported class-retrieval results are strong across several model families, with additional scaling experiments up to 72B parameters. Dataset descriptions, pseudocode, and some training and hardware details provide a useful starting point for reproduction.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification does not establish influence accuracy for actual transformer fine-tuning. Appendix 8.2 treats each distinct input-prefix representation as an independent trainable parameter. In real transformers, these representations depend on shared parameters, so distinct inputs do not eliminate cross-example feature-gradient interactions. Equation (2) is exactly an output-layer gradient inner product before vocabulary truncation; its adequacy as a substitute for full-model or LoRA influence requires evidence that is not supplied. The appendix also reverses the interpretation of its terms: Term (I) comes from gradients with respect to W, whereas Term (II) comes from gradients with respect to hidden features.

The central experiments measure class or template retrieval rather than the stated likelihood change caused by training. Same-class membership is only a proxy for influence, and the benchmarks expose strong class cues: unique chatbot names, repeated math templates, explicit style descriptions, and repeated subject labels. Near-perfect retrieval therefore does not establish accurate influence estimation. Direct comparisons with measured one-step likelihood changes, together with data-selection or removal experiments evaluating subsequent model performance, are needed.

The baseline suite does not sufficiently isolate the contribution. The connection to analytically computed last-layer gradient similarity should be made explicit and evaluated against full-gradient similarity at the same pretrained checkpoint. Simple lexical or template-matching baselines would test whether the retrieval benchmarks require model-based valuation. The Hessian-free baseline uses a single selected checkpoint rather than full checkpoint-aggregated TracIn, so conclusions about that broader method should be limited.

The mislabeled-data experiment does not directly evaluate binary noise detection. Appendix 8.3 defines positives as examples that are both clean and match a particular validation example's class; clean examples from the other class are negatives. This conflates class retrieval with label correctness. A direct clean-versus-corrupted evaluation, including a pretrained-loss or label-confidence baseline, is necessary to substantiate the noise-detection claim.

Important implementation and evaluation details remain unresolved. The top-k cutoff for 'Recall' is unspecified, and its description resembles precision at k unless k equals the number of relevant examples. The meaning of the reported uncertainty and the number of independent runs are not explained. Vocabulary truncation has no accuracy ablation or error analysis; because the retained vocabulary depends on other examples in the batch, scores can depend on batch composition. The paper should specify valuation batch sizes and test ranking stability against full-vocabulary computation.

The efficiency advantage is plausible, but its magnitude is not cleanly established. Table 3 omits sequence-length and forward-inference costs, while runtime comparisons use different hardware allocations and extrapolate some baseline measurements from 10% of validation examples. These results need clearer separation of inference, scoring, and training costs. Overall, the unresolved connection between the score and actual influence, together with the evaluation and reproducibility gaps, prevents a sound Findings recommendation; targeted theoretical clarification and additional experiments could support resubmission next cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical problem: estimating training-data value for LLMs and VLMs without expensive backpropagation or repeated fine-tuning. The proposed score is simple, and its computation from hidden states and prediction errors is clearly specified.

The reported results are promising for class-conditioned retrieval: For-Value achieves near-perfect performance on the synthetic language tasks and substantial improvements on image-style retrieval. Evaluation spans two model families, both language and vision-language models, and scaling experiments up to 72B parameters.

The embedding-only ablation provides evidence that prediction-error alignment contributes substantially to the reported retrieval performance. The algorithm, dataset sources, examples, and some fine-tuning settings provide a useful starting point for reproduction.
weaknesses: The theoretical result does not establish the claimed approximation to actual transformer fine-tuning influence. Equation (2) is exactly the inner product of gradients with respect to the output matrix W, before vocabulary truncation. The proof treats hidden representations for distinct contexts as independent trainable parameters; distinct inputs do not make their parameter gradients independent in a shared transformer. No bound or empirical measurement establishes that the omitted backbone-gradient contribution is small, especially for the attention-layer LoRA updates used by the baselines. Appendix 8.2 also reverses the interpretation of its terms: term (I) comes from differentiation with respect to W, despite being described as the contribution of parameters excluding the unembedding layer.

The main experiments measure same-class retrieval rather than training influence. Class membership is not ground truth for the likelihood change defined in Section 4.1. Shared math templates, identifying chatbot names, explicit style descriptions, and identical subject captions create strong retrieval cues. No controlled update experiment, removal/retraining study, or downstream data-selection experiment verifies that highly ranked examples actually improve validation behavior. This missing connection is decisive for the paper's stated contribution.

The mislabeled-data evaluation does not directly measure clean-versus-corrupted detection. Appendix 8.3 assigns positives only to clean examples whose labels match the validation example; clean examples from another class are negatives alongside corrupted examples. Thus the metric mixes class retrieval and cleanliness. A direct corruption-detection evaluation, including a pretrained-model loss or label-confidence baseline, is needed to establish the claimed benefit.

Important inexpensive controls are absent. Lexical/template similarity would test whether the synthetic benchmarks can be solved through surface overlap, while output-layer gradient similarity at the same checkpoint would clarify the method's relationship to existing first-order estimators. Comparing pretrained For-Value against fine-tuned gradient baselines also changes both the estimator and model state. Selecting baseline checkpoints by highest test AUC favors those baselines, but does not resolve this confounding.

The vocabulary restriction central to efficiency is insufficiently validated. Probability mass outside observed tokens need not be negligible, and changing the batch vocabulary can change an example's score. There is no full-vocabulary comparison, approximation-error analysis, or batch-composition sensitivity study. Table 3 also omits sequence length, valuation-set size, and model inference costs, while runtime comparisons use different GPU counts and extrapolate some baseline timings. The practical speed advantage is plausible, but its magnitude needs a more controlled accounting.

Several reporting details prevent confident reproduction: the top-k cutoff and denominator for 'Recall' are unspecified, the meaning of the reported ± values and number of repeated runs are unclear, and prompt-versus-response scoring masks are not clearly documented. There are also numerical overstatements: Section 6.1 claims the highest subject-generation recall for both VLMs, although Qwen For-Value scores 0.897 versus HyperINF's 0.902. Overall, targeted theoretical clarification and direct influence validation are important revisions before a sound Findings recommendation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: making training-data valuation affordable for LLM and VLM fine-tuning. Computing last-layer gradient inner products from forward-pass representations and prediction errors is simple and practically useful.

The evaluation covers multiple model families, text and multimodal tasks, synthetic corruption, and downstream fine-tuning. The held-out medical evaluations provide the strongest evidence of practical utility: For-Value achieves 62.35 average accuracy on Noise-Huatuo at 10% selection, versus 60.28 for the strongest reported baseline.
The reported valuation runtimes are substantially lower than those of the implemented baselines. The prediction-error ablation also supports using more than unweighted hidden-state similarity.
The manuscript provides explicit scoring equations, pseudocode, dataset statistics, and several training configurations, making the core approach understandable.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution does not establish the claimed approximation to actual LLM/VLM fine-tuning dynamics. Appendix B replaces the shared neural network with independently trainable contextual feature vectors and an unembedding matrix. Distinct inputs eliminate feature-gradient interactions in this surrogate, but not in a transformer whose parameters are shared across inputs. Equation (1) is a last-layer gradient inner product; no approximation bound or direct empirical comparison with actual likelihood changes establishes that it captures full-model influence. Furthermore, the discussion following Equation (7) reverses the interpretation of the terms: Term (I) comes from gradients of W, while Term (II) comes from feature gradients.

The GSM8K experiment uses test reasoning examples as valuation data and then reports accuracy on that test set. This explicitly test-informed selection can demonstrate adaptation to known targets, but cannot establish ordinary held-out generalization. Appendix A.3 also describes full-dataset warm-up before subset fine-tuning, making the claim about training on only 1% or 5% of the data potentially misleading. A separate valuation split and an unambiguous training protocol are needed.

Most influence-identification results measure same-class retrieval rather than actual training influence. The synthetic tasks expose class identity through repeated templates, unique chatbot names, and explicit subject/style labels. Near-perfect AUC therefore does not validate the causal interpretation of the scores. Small-scale retraining or measured one-step likelihood-change experiments, together with lexical/template-matching controls, would provide much stronger evidence.

The downstream comparisons lack random subsets and inexpensive loss/perplexity-based selection baselines. These are particularly important for detecting synthetic word insertion/deletion and flipped labels in tasks already familiar to pretrained models. Baselines also differ in checkpoint and parameterization: for PMC, For-Value uses the pretrained model while competing methods use warmed-up LoRA models. Matched-checkpoint comparisons are needed to isolate the scoring method. Tables 3–5 provide no repeated-run uncertainty, which limits interpretation of modest improvements such as 52.23 versus 51.60 on PMC.

The sparse-vocabulary approximation central to scalability is insufficiently validated. Restricting prediction errors to tokens appearing in the current batch drops contributions from other vocabulary items and makes a pair's score depend on unrelated batch members. The paper provides neither retained-probability measurements nor comparisons against exact scores, ranking stability, or batch-size/order sensitivity.

Efficiency claims exceed the demonstrated evidence. Per-example gradients do not inherently require batch size one, and Hessian-free gradient similarity does not inherently require convergence. Appendix A.1 also specifies four GPUs for large-model inference despite the main text's single-GPU framing, and some baseline timings are extrapolated. Matched hardware, explicit inclusion of warm-up/inference/scoring costs, peak memory, and batch-throughput measurements would make the speed claims more reliable.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the submitted PDF says code is available at GitHub but supplies no usable repository URL; the top-k cutoff for the reported Recall metric is unspecified; and checkpoint/warm-up descriptions do not consistently match the initialization-only framing. These issues, together with the theoretical and evaluation concerns above, prevent a sound Findings recommendation at present. The practical method is promising, and focused revisions and additional controls could plausibly support resubmission next cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem: reducing the computational cost of selecting useful fine-tuning data for LLMs and VLMs. Computing output-layer gradient similarities directly from hidden states and prediction errors is a practical way to avoid backpropagation.

The evaluation spans several model families, text and multimodal tasks, and downstream fine-tuning. The medical experiments use separate valuation data and held-out benchmarks, providing evidence beyond synthetic retrieval tasks. For example, Table 4 reports 62.35 average accuracy versus 60.28 for the strongest competing method at 10% selection.
The reported valuation runtimes suggest useful efficiency gains. The algorithm is reasonably clear, and the appendix supplies dataset sizes, task templates, and several training configurations.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification does not establish the claimed approximation to actual fine-tuning influence. Appendix B replaces the shared transformer with independently trainable hidden representations and an unembedding matrix. Distinct inputs eliminate feature-gradient interactions in this surrogate, but not in a real transformer with shared parameters. Equation (1) is an output-layer gradient inner product; neither an approximation bound nor direct agreement with measured fine-tuning effects is provided. Moreover, the explanation following Equations (6)–(7) reverses the roles of the terms: Term (I) arises from gradients of the unembedding matrix, despite being described as excluding that layer.

The GSM8K experiment explicitly uses test reasoning examples as valuation data, with all 1,319 test examples listed in Table 11. Consequently, the reported test accuracy measures selection with access to test targets, rather than generalization to an untouched test set. This can support an explicitly oracle attribution experiment, but it does not substantiate the broader practical data-selection claim. A separate validation set is needed.

Most influence-identification results measure same-class retrieval rather than actual training influence. The synthetic tasks contain strong class cues, including unique chatbot names, repeated mathematical templates, explicit style descriptions, and identical subject answers. Near-perfect retrieval therefore does not establish that scores predict changes in model behavior. Controlled updates or removal experiments, together with lexical and answer-overlap baselines, would substantially strengthen this evidence.

The downstream comparisons lack random selection at matched subset sizes and simple loss-based selection, making it difficult to establish the benefit of valuation over inexpensive alternatives. Tables 3–5 also omit uncertainty across selection and training seeds; this particularly matters for the 0.5-point improvement over full-data GSM8K training and the 0.63-point advantage over HyperINF on 10% PMC data. At 20% PMC selection, HyperINF performs better.

Checkpoint and training differences confound the comparison. Appendix A.3 uses LoRA warm-up for baselines, full-parameter warm-up for For-Value on GSM8K, and a pretrained checkpoint for For-Value on PMC. Thus, the experiments change both the scoring method and the representation being scored. GSM8K also exposes the model to the full training set before subset fine-tuning, which limits claims about training with only 5% of the data. Matched-checkpoint ablations and clearly separated warm-up, valuation, and fine-tuning costs are needed.

The vocabulary restriction in Equation (2) introduces an unvalidated approximation central to scalability. No retained-probability-mass analysis, comparison with full-vocabulary scores, or ranking-stability study is reported. Since the retained vocabulary depends on other examples in the batch, scores can also depend on batch composition. The complexity analysis omits sequence-length and valuation-set dependence, while the claim that gradient methods necessarily require batch size one is too categorical.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. The manuscript states that code is available at GitHub but provides no usable repository link. Recall is described without specifying the retrieval cutoff, and valuation batch sizes, seed counts, and some checkpoint details remain unclear. The main text describes single-GPU scaling, whereas Appendix A.1 uses four GPUs for large-model inference and extrapolates some baseline runtimes. These unresolved methodological and reporting issues prevent a sound Findings recommendation, although the practical approach appears promising enough for a revised submission next cycle.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical problem: reducing the cost of training-data valuation for LLMs and VLMs. Computing output-layer gradient similarities from forward-pass quantities is simple, interpretable, and potentially useful.

The experiments cover multiple model families, language and vision-language tasks, and downstream fine-tuning. The held-out medical evaluations provide the strongest evidence of practical utility: For-Value achieves 62.35% average accuracy on Noise-Huatuo at 10% selection, versus 60.28% for HyperINF, with substantially lower reported valuation time.

The prediction-error ablation supports using more than hidden-state similarity alone. The paper also provides pseudocode, dataset descriptions, training settings, and an explicit derivation, making the proposed approach reasonably accessible.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim exceeds what the derivation establishes. Equation (1) is an output-layer gradient inner product. Appendix B obtains its sufficiency by replacing the transformer with independently trainable features for distinct inputs; expressivity alone does not establish that this surrogate reproduces shared-parameter transformer training dynamics. Distinct inputs do not eliminate cross-example feature-gradient interactions in an actual transformer. No approximation bound or direct comparison against measured likelihood changes establishes the claimed accuracy. Moreover, Appendix B reverses the interpretation of terms (I) and (II): term (I) comes from gradients of the unembedding matrix W, contrary to the accompanying explanation.

Most influence-identification experiments measure same-class retrieval rather than actual training influence. The synthetic templates, explicit transformation identifiers, and shared subject/style labels make semantic or lexical matching a plausible explanation for near-perfect results. The mislabeled-data metric likewise combines class matching with cleanliness. These are useful proxy tasks, but direct one-step loss-change or retraining-based influence validation is needed to substantiate the central claim.

The GSM8K experiment explicitly uses test reasoning examples for valuation and then reports accuracy on that test set. This is a disclosed test-informed selection experiment, not an independent generalization evaluation. A separate valuation split and untouched test set are needed. Appendix A.3 also describes full-dataset warm-up training, so the reported 1%/5% selection results require clearer accounting of prior exposure to the remaining training data.

The downstream comparisons lack random-subset and simple loss/perplexity selection controls, and Tables 3–5 do not report uncertainty across fine-tuning runs. Consequently, the added value over inexpensive selection strategies and the reliability of smaller gains remain unclear. Scoring checkpoints and parameterizations also differ between methods; a matched-checkpoint comparison would better isolate the proposed scoring rule.

The sparse implementation introduces an additional unvalidated approximation. Restricting prediction errors to tokens appearing in the samples can discard probability mass, and the in-batch vocabulary makes an example's score potentially depend on its batch companions. The paper provides neither dense-versus-sparse ranking agreement nor sensitivity to batch composition, vocabulary size, or sequence length. These checks matter because the efficient implementation is central to the contribution.

Efficiency and reproducibility claims need tighter reporting. The main text describes single-GPU scaling, while Appendix A.1 uses four A100s for larger-model inference and extrapolates some baseline timings. Claims that gradient methods inherently require batch size one are too strong. Report matched hardware, total GPU-hours, warm-up costs, peak memory, and batch-size scaling. The manuscript's code-availability statement contains no identifiable repository link, and recall cutoffs, random seeds, and some checkpoint choices remain insufficiently specified. Together with the theoretical and evaluation concerns, these are important revisions that prevent a clear Findings recommendation in the current form.
